byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: Nine in ten Indians lived in villages in a year when famine and plague both ran their course; the population count is in the history and economy section.

items.title: Town and village
items.summary: Roughly nine in ten people lived in villages and about one in ten in towns.

sources.label: People's Archive of Rural India: Report on the Census of India, 1901 (summary of the Risley and Gait report)

items.metric: Share of people living in towns

items.title: Literate in English
items.summary: Only 68 of every 10,000 men and 7 of every 10,000 women could read English; the summary gives no figure for literacy in all languages.

sources.label: People's Archive of Rural India: Report on the Census of India, 1901 (summary of the Risley and Gait report)

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: At the start of the century a newborn in India could expect to live only about 24 years.

sources.label: MoSPI: Table 2.9, Life expectancy at birth, India
Factodata: Life expectancy in India, growth over the years

items.title: Rail passengers
items.summary: More than 175 million passenger journeys were made on about 25,000 miles of track in 1900.

sources.label: ThePrint: West sees overcrowded trains as a classic Indian trope, but they are a colonial relic
Brewminate: Overcrowded trains, a relic of colonialism and capitalism in India

items.title: Bombay's shrinking count
items.summary: Bombay city's census population fell from 820,000 in 1891 to 780,000 in 1901 as plague drove people away.

sources.label: TIFR: The Plague Epidemics of the 1890s (Bombay history)

sensitivity.note: This item describes famine, epidemic disease or loss of life.

byTheNumbers.scarcityNote: Household electricity, telephones and household size are not available for 1900. The figures below are those we could trace to a source.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: The staple depended on the region: rice in the east, millets and pulses for the poor across much of the north and west, with wheat and white rice on richer tables.

items.title: A staple for every region
items.summary: Bengal and Orissa ate rice, mostly coarse early rice among the poor; in the Punjab, the North-Western Provinces, Oudh, Bihar and Gujarat the poor lived on millets and pulses, and wheat and rice were for the better off.

sources.label: National Library of Scotland: Sanitation, Diet, Disease (early-twentieth-century India)

items.title: Barley, bajra and husked millets
items.summary: In the Delhi region barley, bajra and husked millets were eaten across castes and classes, while elite households ate wheat and white rice.

sources.label: IIT Delhi: Avadh food cultures

items.title: What rice cost
items.summary: The price of rice is on the Prices board as 11.7 seers to the rupee (1896-1900 average).

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. III: Economic (1907), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive

foodAndKitchen.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1900 meal patterns, kitchen tools or food storage practice, so this section is short.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: Cloth came from two worlds: the hand loom, which held its place, and the new Bombay mills.

items.title: Bombay's mills
items.summary: Bombay's first cotton mill opened in 1854, and by 1900 more than 84 had been set up in the city, mostly by Parsi and Gujarati entrepreneurs.

sources.label: GKToday: Cotton textile industry in colonial India

items.title: The hand loom survives
items.summary: Hand-loom weaving did not die out; its share of the cloth market stayed roughly stable between the 1890s and the 1930s, because machines could not make some kinds of cloth.

sources.label: Cambridge University Press: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India, chapter on handloom weaving

clothingAndStyle.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced descriptions of everyday garments, fabrics bought or fashions of 1900.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: Most people worked the land; in the famine year the state paid relief wages below market rates.

items.title: An agricultural labourer
items.summary: An able-bodied agricultural labourer earned on average Rs 6.5 to 7.0 a month across India in 1896-1900.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. III: Economic (1907), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive

items.originalUnits: Rs 6.5 to 7.0 per month (rupees, annas and pies; 16 annas = 1 rupee)

items.title: Relief work and its pay
items.summary: Famine relief followed the Famine Code of 1883, but relief wages were set below market rates, and a new famine commission produced a revised code in 1901.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Indian famine of 1899-1900

sensitivity.note: This item describes famine, epidemic disease or loss of life.

items.title: A fifth on relief
items.summary: By July 1900 about one-fifth of the Central Provinces' population was on some form of famine relief.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Indian famine of 1899-1900

sensitivity.note: This item describes famine, epidemic disease or loss of life.

workAndWages.scarcityNote: Wage rates are hard to trace for 1900. The one sourced figure is the agricultural labourer's average; we did not estimate others.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: Village pathshalas and madrasas coexisted with government and mission schools, and few children reached any school.

items.title: Schools in the Bombay Presidency
items.summary: In 1902-03 the Presidency had 12,218 educational institutions with 599,708 pupils, down from 12,251 institutions and 639,868 pupils a year earlier.

sources.label: Report on the Administration of the Bombay Presidency for 1902-03 (Qatar Digital Library)

items.metric: Pupils in Bombay Presidency educational institutions

items.title: A few in a hundred
items.summary: In the Bombay Presidency the share of the population under instruction rose from 2.3 to 2.6 percent in 1904-05, and reached 3.3 percent by 1909-10.

sources.label: Report on the Administration of the Bombay Presidency for 1904-05 (Qatar Digital Library)
Annual Report of the Administration of the Bombay Presidency, 1909-10 (Qatar Digital Library)

items.title: The village pathshala
items.summary: Village pathshalas met under a tree, in a shop, a temple or the teacher's house with no fixed timetable and paused for the harvest; after 1854 government pandits introduced textbooks, timetables and annual exams.

sources.label: PW: CBSE Class 8 History notes, Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

schoolAndChildhood.scarcityNote: We could not find all-India school counts or school fees for 1900; the figures here are for the Bombay Presidency.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: Most journeys by rail were third class, crowded and cheap per mile; roads still belonged to the bullock cart.

items.title: Nine in ten rode third class
items.summary: Third-class passengers made up almost nine in ten of rail travellers, in overcrowded and unsanitary carriages.

sources.label: ThePrint: West sees overcrowded trains as a classic Indian trope, but they are a colonial relic
Brewminate: Overcrowded trains, a relic of colonialism and capitalism in India

items.title: Pies per mile
items.summary: On the East Indian Railway the third-class fare was about 2.5 pies per mile for the first 100 miles, falling further beyond.

sources.label: Roger Farnworth: Railways and Tramways Blog (EIR), quoting Huddleston

gettingAround.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1900 fares or journey times for named routes, so there are no journey cards.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: A quarter-anna postcard had opened letter-writing to millions since 1879.

items.title: The quarter-anna postcard
items.summary: The Indian post introduced a quarter-anna postcard in July 1879 for use within British India; a card for countries of the Universal Postal Union cost one and a half annas.

sources.label: India TV News: India book traces history of picture postcards
iStampGallery: India on Post Card

items.title: Twenty-six million cards
items.summary: By 1883 about 26 million postcards a year were being sold in India, and reply cards followed in 1890.

sources.label: India TV News: India book traces history of picture postcards
Outlook Traveller: In pictures, India through postcards

keepingInTouch.scarcityNote: We could not find 1900 letter rates, post-office counts or telegram rates, and no delivery times; there are no message cards.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: Plague and famine marked the year, and the plague laboratory at Parel was a young institution.

items.title: Plague in Bombay
items.summary: Plague was first detected in Bombay in September 1896; the city answered with house searches, isolation of the sick, camps for travellers and forced evacuation of residents, and the plague death rate in 1900 was about 22 per thousand.

sources.label: TIFR: The Plague Epidemics of the 1890s (Bombay history)
Wikipedia: Bombay plague epidemic

sensitivity.note: This item describes famine, epidemic disease or loss of life.

items.title: The plague laboratory
items.summary: A plague research laboratory set up at J. J. Hospital moved in 1899 to Government House in Parel under Dr W. M. Haffkine, the start of the Haffkine Institute.

sources.label: TIFR: The Plague Epidemics of the 1890s (Bombay history)
PubMed Central: Plague in Bombay, Haffkine Serum

healthAndMedicine.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1900 doctor fees, hospital costs or common remedies for India; the famine itself is in the history section.

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: The public Ganesh festival of Pune, begun in the early 1890s, was one of the new ways of celebrating together.

items.title: The public Ganesh festival
items.summary: Ganesh Chaturthi, once mostly kept at home, became a large public festival in Pune in the 1890s; sources date the first public idol to 1892 or 1893, and Lokmanya Tilak promoted it through his paper Kesari.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Ganesh Chaturthi
Brut India: Ganesh Chaturthi was once mostly a private celebration

leisureAndFun.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced material on cinema shows, wrestling, cricket outings or other festivals as people practised them in 1900.

spotlight.title: Rail, post and telegraph in daily life
spotlight.standfirst: By 1900 the railway, the quarter-anna postcard and the telegraph had tied the country together for those who could afford them.

items.title: The telegraph
items.summary: The telegraph network grew from a first line of 82 miles in 1851 to 78,862 miles of line by the end of 1913.

sources.label: The Sunday-school Times / Signs of the Times, 17 November 1914 (Adventist Archives)

spotlight.scarcityNote: Rail and post are covered under Getting around and Keeping in touch; we could not find a sourced 1900 count of post offices, letters carried or telegraph mileage.
